summary:
Missouri's Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 after a judge denied a preliminary injunction sought by Lambda Legal, the ACLU of Missouri and Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner, who had filed in Cole County Circuit Court on behalf of three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA. The law bars under-18s from starting hormones or puberty blockers, though those already in treatment may continue, and prohibits all transition-related surgery for minors.

The SAFE Act also bars Missouri HealthNet Medicaid from covering gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes violating providers to medical-licence revocation. Doctors who breach the ban can also be sued by patients up to 15 years after treatment.

The ban has been upheld twice. Judge Robert Craig Carter ruled it constitutional on 25 November 2024 after a September 2024 trial in the 44th Judicial Circuit Court, with plaintiffs announcing an appeal; on 13 January 2026 the Missouri Supreme Court upheld the ban unanimously, citing the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court decision upholding Tennessee's similar law. The statute sunsets on 28 August 2027, but lawmakers seek to make it permanent and a November 2026 ballot initiative also aims to extend the ban indefinitely.

Trans inmates in Missouri state prisons face a separate care cutoff. Effective 2 July 2026, an appropriations law signed by Governor Mike Kehoe bars state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Missouri became the seventh state, and the second in 2026 after Oklahoma, to ban such care for incarcerated people; Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical laws, while federal courts blocked comparable Idaho and Georgia measures.

Missouri restricts sports participation by sex assigned at birth. Senate Bill 39, signed 7 June 2023, requires public and private schools through college to limit sports to sex assigned at birth, and a May 2023 law bans transgender athletes from female sports with a sunset clause repealing it on 28 August 2027.

Changing identity documents in Missouri requires surgery or a court order. Under Mo. Ann. Stat. § 193.215(9), a birth certificate sex change requires a court order supported by certified proof on hospital letterhead stating that the petitioner's physical sex has been altered and the surgical changes are irreversible. Two 2013 cases that had allowed exceptions were invalidated and reversed in May 2022, leaving no workaround to the surgical requirement. Between 2016 and 2024 the Department of Revenue accepted Form 5532 for gender designation changes on licences or IDs, then reverted to requiring surgery documentation or a court order after an unspecified incident.

Missouri's hate-crime statutes explicitly cover gender identity, defined as "having a self-image or identity not traditionally associated with one's gender," but the state's non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity. The state operates a tipline for anonymous reporting of suspected violations of the SAFE Act and complaints about "gender transition intervention." Kansas City declared itself a sanctuary city for transgender individuals in May 2023, and Columbia voted in February 2024 to include LGBT protections in its sanctuary ordinance.
tangentialFactors:
Missouri's care ban sits within a wider national pattern: gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and several states have moved to extend such bans to incarcerated adults. Missouri's inmate-care restriction is one of seven such state laws, and federal courts have blocked comparable measures in Idaho and Georgia, so the operative position in neighbouring jurisdictions differs.

Missouri's document rules are stricter than in some states. Equality-map research shows conditions for changing a gender marker on a licence or birth certificate vary state by state, and Missouri's surgical requirement, reinstated after a 2022 court reversal, is among the more restrictive.

The SAFE Act's 2027 sunset and the pending November 2026 ballot initiative mean the legal position on youth care is subject to change; the ban is currently moving toward permanence rather than being struck down.
localsOnly:
Missouri residents under 18 cannot begin gender-affirming hormones or puberty blockers under the SAFE Act, though those already receiving care before 28 August 2023 may continue until the law's 2027 sunset. Providers who violate the ban risk medical-licence revocation and civil suits filed up to 15 years after treatment.

Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming care is barred for patients of any age in Missouri. Trans inmates in state prisons lost state-funded hormone therapy and transition surgery as of 2 July 2026, with no taper for those already in treatment.

Birth certificate sex changes require a court order with certified hospital proof of irreversible surgical alteration under § 193.215(9); the Department of Revenue requires surgery documentation or a court order for gender designation changes on licences and IDs. Missouri hate-crime law covers gender identity, but the state's non-discrimination statutes do not.

In April 2023 the Attorney General issued an emergency order declaring adult gender-affirming care experimental and imposing extensive psychiatric and documentation requirements; a judge temporarily blocked it and it was withdrawn in May 2023. A related March–April 2023 order on youth care was also withdrawn on 16 May 2023.

The outcome of the plaintiffs' appeal of the November 2024 trial-court ruling was resolved by the Missouri Supreme Court's January 2026 upholding, but any further appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court is not sourced here.

Whether the November 2026 ballot initiative to make the SAFE Act permanent has been placed on the ballot or its result is unresolved in the source inventory.

The "unspecified incident" that prompted the Department of Revenue to reverse its Form 5532 policy is not detailed in the sources; the current documentation requirement is stated, but the trigger is not.

Whether Missouri's prison-care cutoff has been challenged in court, as comparable Idaho and Georgia measures were, is not sourced.
